# Cross-Controller Comparison: PV–BESS Dispatch Strategies
### v2 Model — Glasgow 2023

---

## 1. Overview

This report compares three battery dispatch strategies applied to the Stage 2
PV–BESS model for a Glasgow household over the full 2023 calendar year. The
purpose is to contextualise the MILP optimum against two rules-based
alternatives that reflect real domestic battery control implementations, and
to quantify the economic value of optimisation relative to simpler heuristics.

**System specification:** 4 kWp PV (PVGIS SARAH-3, 2023), 10 kWh / 3 kW
battery, η_c = η_d = 0.95, SOC window 10–90%, degradation cost 5 p/kWh cycled,
Octopus Agile half-hourly tariff 2023 (import and export). Household demand
4,920 kWh/yr (CREST synthetic profile). All three controllers operate on the
same input data; the MILP schedule is loaded from the Stage 2 annual run.

---

## 2. Controller Descriptions

### 2.1 Controller A — PV Self-Consumption Only

Controller A represents the simplest sensible domestic battery mode: the
battery stores PV surplus and discharges to cover demand deficit. It never
draws from the grid to charge the battery, and it has no awareness of the
Agile tariff signal. The same decision rule applies at every half-hour of
every day:

- **PV surplus** (generation > demand): charge the battery from surplus at the
  full available rate; export any remainder.
- **Demand deficit** (demand > generation): discharge the battery at the full
  available rate; import any remainder.

This is price-agnostic by design. All battery cycling is driven solely by the
instantaneous PV–demand balance, so the battery is only ever cycled on
effectively free solar energy. In winter months with minimal Glasgow irradiance,
the battery is nearly idle.

### 2.2 Controller B — Fixed Agile Price Threshold

Controller B represents a simple Agile-aware heuristic, replicating the
behaviour of real domestic battery systems with Agile integration (e.g.
GivEnergy Timed Charge, Tesla Powerwall Time-Based Control). A single threshold
*T* (p/kWh) governs all decisions, applied greedily one half-hour at a time
with no look-ahead:

- **import\_price ≤ T** (price is cheap): grid-charge the battery at the full
  available rate. Any PV present reduces the import requirement; if PV exceeds
  demand + charge, the surplus is exported.
- **import\_price > T and PV surplus**: self-consume — store surplus PV in the
  battery, export any remainder.
- **import\_price > T and demand deficit**: discharge the battery to reduce
  import; import any unmet remainder.
- **Otherwise** (no battery headroom): serve demand directly from the grid.

The threshold *T* was swept from 5 to 30 p/kWh in 5 p steps, and the value
maximising the annual net saving was selected (see Section 4).

### 2.3 MILP Optimal (brief)

The MILP formulation jointly optimises all 48 half-hourly charge, discharge,
import and export decisions simultaneously for each day, with full knowledge of
the day's Agile price profile. An import/export binary variable prevents
simultaneous grid import and export. A throughput-based degradation penalty is
embedded directly in the objective. Full formulation details are given in
`docs/v2_model_report.md` and `src/model.py`. The MILP schedule used here was
produced by the Stage 2 annual rolling-horizon runner (`scripts/run_stage2.py`).

---

## 3. Annual Results

| Controller | Import cost (£) | Export rev (£) | Degrad cost (£) | Net energy cost (£) | Annual saving (£) | Simple payback |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| No battery (counterfactual) | 893 | 199 | — | 693 | — | — |
| **Controller A** (PV self-consume) | 544 | 52 | 145 | 492 | **56** | 71.3 yr |
| **Controller B** (T = 5 p/kWh, best) | 487 | 57 | 174 | 431 | **89** | 45.2 yr |
| **MILP optimal** | 499 | 118 | 157 | 381 | **155** | 25.8 yr |

*Annual saving = counterfactual net cost − (battery net energy cost + degradation cost).
Battery capital cost assumed £4,000. Degradation cost 5 p/kWh cycled (optimistic LFP assumption).*

All three strategies are economically unviable at this capital cost and
degradation assumption — the best achievable payback (MILP, 25.8 yr) far
exceeds the expected battery service life. However, the comparison reveals
a clear ordering and the sources of value at each level of sophistication.

---

## 4. Controller B — Threshold Sensitivity

The figure below shows how Controller B's annual saving varies with the
threshold *T*. Controller A (self-consumption) and MILP horizontal reference
lines are shown for comparison.

![Controller B threshold sensitivity](<data:image/png;base64,>)

The saving falls sharply above T = 5 p/kWh and turns negative by T = 20 p/kWh.
This reflects a structural feature of the 2023 Agile data: overnight prices in
2023 were consistently elevated (13–25 p/kWh) due to the energy crisis, so any
threshold above 5 p/kWh triggers frequent grid-charging at prices that are not
cheap enough to justify the round-trip losses and degradation cost. At T = 5 p/kWh,
the controller only charges when prices dip below 5 p (or go negative), which
happens rarely in 2023 and captures most of the genuine arbitrage value without
expensive cycling at intermediate prices.

---

## 5. Representative Day Dispatch

Two representative days are examined: a winter day (10 January 2023) with
minimal PV generation and elevated Agile prices, and a summer day (1 July 2023)
with strong PV surplus. All plots follow the same format: upper panel shows
power flows (kW, left axis) and SOC (fraction, right axis); lower panel shows
the Agile import and export prices (p/kWh) with the degradation cost reference
line (dotted blue at 5 p/kWh).

### 5.1 Winter Day — 10 January 2023

**Controller A (PV self-consumption only)**

![Controller A — 10 January 2023](<data:image/png;base64,>)

With negligible PV in a Scottish January (orange line barely visible above zero),
the battery has no surplus to store and so sits at its minimum SOC throughout
the entire day. Demand is met entirely by direct grid import. The controller
correctly does nothing — no wasted cycling, no degradation cost incurred.

**Controller B (T = 5 p/kWh)**

![Controller B — 10 January 2023](<data:image/png;base64,>)

Controller B is similarly inactive for most of the day: import prices on
10 January 2023 stay above 5 p/kWh through the morning and afternoon. The
battery only acts in the final half-hours of the day when prices briefly dip
toward or below 5 p/kWh (visible as the small charge/discharge spike near
23:30). Demand is met by direct grid import for the vast majority of the day.

**MILP optimal**

![MILP optimal — 10 January 2023](<data:image/png;base64,>)

The MILP identifies and exploits the few half-hours with a price spread
sufficient to cover round-trip losses plus degradation (visible as targeted
charge/discharge events aligned with price dips and peaks in the lower panel).
Outside these windows it imports directly. The MILP's advantage over both
rules-based controllers is most evident in winter, where price-signal
exploitation is the only available source of value.

### 5.2 Summer Day — 1 July 2023

**Controller A (PV self-consumption only)**

![Controller A — 1 July 2023](<data:image/png;base64,>)

This is the canonical PV self-consumption profile. The battery charges from PV
surplus from approximately 06:00 onwards (blue charge line), with SOC rising to
near the maximum by mid-morning. Once full, excess PV is exported (green dashed
line tracks the PV curve). From mid-afternoon the battery discharges steadily to
serve evening demand (purple discharge line), delaying grid import until
approximately 21:30. The battery is only ever cycled on free solar, and the
lower panel confirms the controller is entirely indifferent to the price signal.

**Controller B (T = 5 p/kWh)**

![Controller B — 1 July 2023](<data:image/png;base64,>)

Controller B's dispatch on a summer day is broadly similar to Controller A
except that brief grid-charging occurs during any half-hours where the import
price drops below 5 p/kWh, supplementing the PV self-consumption strategy
with the occasional opportunistic charge. The effect is modest on this
particular day; the difference between B and A accumulates mainly from
negative-price events distributed across the year.

**MILP optimal**

![MILP optimal — 1 July 2023](<data:image/png;base64,>)

The MILP's summer dispatch shows a more active arbitrage strategy layered on
top of self-consumption. It coordinates PV capture, selective grid-charging
during cheap morning half-hours, and targeted discharge during peak-price
evening periods in a pattern that cannot be replicated by a greedy heuristic
operating without look-ahead. Export revenue is also higher than for either
rules-based controller (visible from the larger green export spikes), because
the MILP can plan ahead to leave headroom for PV rather than pre-charging
the battery at suboptimal prices.

---

## 6. Discussion

### 6.1 PV self-consumption value is modest but positive

Controller A achieves a £56/yr saving solely through PV self-consumption and
evening discharge, with no grid interaction beyond meeting residual demand. The
saving is positive — removing the overnight grid-charging that was present in
the original "timer" design eliminates the destructive cycling at energy-crisis
prices — but the 71-year payback confirms that PV self-consumption alone
cannot justify the capital cost of a domestic battery at 2023 Agile conditions.

### 6.2 Price-threshold control offers limited additional value

Controller B's best threshold (T = 5 p/kWh) adds only £33/yr over Controller A,
raising the annual saving to £89 (45-year payback). The threshold sweep
demonstrates that raising T beyond 5 p/kWh rapidly destroys value, because the
2023 Agile market — still elevated from the 2021–22 energy crisis — offered
very few overnight periods cheap enough to justify battery cycling once
degradation cost is included. In a pre-crisis year with typical overnight
Agile dips to 2–6 p/kWh, a higher threshold would have been beneficial.

### 6.3 Perfect-foresight MILP captures 75 % more value than the best heuristic

The MILP achieves £155/yr (25.8-year payback) — a **£66/yr (75%) uplift** over
Controller B at its optimal threshold. This gap quantifies the value of
look-ahead optimisation under a volatile tariff: the MILP avoids loss-making
cycles that a greedy controller cannot anticipate, exploits short favourable
price windows that fall below any fixed threshold only briefly, and coordinates
import/export to maximise export revenue. This uplift is the central
model-derived finding of this work.

### 6.4 Economic viability under 2023 conditions

Under all three strategies, and even under perfect foresight, the system is
economically unviable at a £4,000 capital cost with 5 p/kWh degradation.
The MILP's 25.8-year payback represents a theoretical best case for the
2023 Glasgow / Agile scenario. The v3 parameter study will explore whether
different locations, system sizes, tariff structures, or lower capital costs
can push the payback period into a commercially viable range.

---

## 7. Conclusions

| Finding | Value |
|---|---|
| PV self-consumption saving (Controller A) | £56/yr |
| Best heuristic saving (Controller B, T = 5 p) | £89/yr |
| MILP optimal saving | £155/yr |
| MILP uplift over best heuristic | +£66/yr (+75%) |
| MILP payback (Glasgow, Agile 2023, 10 kWh, 5 p/kWh deg) | 25.8 yr |
| Economically viable at £4,000 capex? | No (all controllers) |

The comparison establishes that the MILP formulation captures materially more
value than any implementable heuristic under the 2023 Agile tariff, and that
the dominant barrier to viability is the capital cost of the battery rather than
the sophistication of the control strategy. A simpler self-consumption
controller achieves approximately one-third of the MILP optimum, confirming
that PV self-consumption is a real but insufficient source of value under these
conditions.
